overviewHtml:
This ungraded knowledge check assesses your understanding of what the evidence shows about AI's effect on jobs. You'll be asked about exposure and displacement, productivity evidence at two scales, the two positions on job loss, and the finding on entry-level employment.

Note: Use this to test yourself, review the feedback on any questions you miss, and retry until you feel confident before moving forward.

forms.stemHtml: A news story says a study found that 80 percent of workers are "exposed" to AI. What does that figure describe?

options.html: The share of workers who will lose their jobs within a few years
options.text: The share of workers who will lose their jobs within a few years
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Exposure studies make no prediction about job loss or timing. The figure describes the share of workers with some tasks that AI could do or speed up.

options.html: The share of workers whose employers have already adopted AI tools
options.text: The share of workers whose employers have already adopted AI tools
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Exposure describes what is technically possible, not what employers have done. The figure describes the share of workers with some tasks that AI could do or speed up.

options.html: The share of workers with some tasks that AI could do or speed up
options.text: The share of workers with some tasks that AI could do or speed up
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Exposure is a judgment about which tasks AI could affect. It doesn't say whether those tasks will be automated, augmented, or rearranged, or when.

options.html: The share of workers whose pay has fallen since AI chatbots appeared
options.text: The share of workers whose pay has fallen since AI chatbots appeared
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Exposure studies don't measure pay. The figure describes the share of workers with some tasks that AI could do or speed up.

forms.stemHtml: Experiments find productivity gains of about 14 percent in customer support, while one economist estimates that AI will add less than 1 percent to economy-wide productivity over ten years. What best explains how both can be right?

options.html: A large gain on a small share of all tasks is small overall
options.text: A large gain on a small share of all tasks is small overall
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The economy-wide estimate multiplies the gain per task by the share of tasks affected. Few tasks are affected so far, adoption takes time, and the easiest tasks were studied first.

options.html: The experiments were run by companies and can be disregarded
options.text: The experiments were run by companies and can be disregarded
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Both sides accept the task-level results. The figures differ because a large gain on a small share of all tasks is small overall.

options.html: The economist measured a different country from the experiments
options.text: The economist measured a different country from the experiments
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The difference isn't about geography. A large gain on a small share of all tasks is small overall.

options.html: Productivity in customer support has no bearing on the economy
options.text: Productivity in customer support has no bearing on the economy
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Customer support is part of the economy, and its gains count. They are a small part of the total, because a large gain on a small share of all tasks is small overall.

forms.stemHtml: What does the no-displacement position mainly rely on?

options.html: Payroll records showing that young workers are being hired faster
options.text: Payroll records showing that young workers are being hired faster
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Payroll records show a gap for young workers in exposed occupations, not faster hiring. The position mainly relies on the record of earlier technologies.

options.html: Exposure studies showing that few occupations contain exposed tasks
options.text: Exposure studies showing that few occupations contain exposed tasks
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Exposure studies find wide exposure. The position mainly relies on the record of earlier technologies, which created more jobs than they destroyed.

options.html: Experiments showing that AI gives no productivity gain on any task
options.text: Experiments showing that AI gives no productivity gain on any task
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Task-level experiments do show gains. The position mainly relies on the record of earlier technologies, which created more jobs than they destroyed.

options.html: The record of earlier technologies, which created more jobs overall
options.text: The record of earlier technologies, which created more jobs overall
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Advocates such as Andrew Ng argue that the pattern of earlier technologies will hold. That is real evidence about the past and no guarantee about AI.

forms.stemHtml: A Stanford study of payroll records found employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations 19 percent below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers. Which statements about this finding are accurate? (Select all that apply.)

options.html: The authors call it descriptive and not a causal estimate
options.text: The authors call it descriptive and not a causal estimate
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! They describe their results as early, descriptive indicators.

options.html: Experienced workers in the same occupations show no comparable gap
options.text: Experienced workers in the same occupations show no comparable gap
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The gap is specific to workers at the start of their careers.

options.html: It shows that 19 percent of young workers were laid off because of AI
options.text: It shows that 19 percent of young workers were laid off because of AI
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The figure is a gap relative to a comparison group, it comes mainly from reduced hiring, and the authors don't claim AI caused it.

options.html: Critics attribute the pattern to rising interest rates
options.text: Critics attribute the pattern to rising interest rates
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! Economists at Google argue that hiring in these occupations began falling in 2022, before AI chatbots were widely used.

forms.stemHtml: An analysis of economy-wide United States data found no significant effect of AI on employment as of May 2026. A payroll study found a gap for young workers in exposed occupations. How do these two results relate?

options.html: The economy-wide result proves the payroll finding is mistaken
options.text: The economy-wide result proves the payroll finding is mistaken
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The economy-wide data is weak at detecting effects in small groups. An effect limited to one small group can be real and not show up in the totals.

options.html: An effect in one small group may not show in economy-wide totals
options.text: An effect in one small group may not show in economy-wide totals
options.feedbackHtml: Correct! The authors of the economy-wide analysis say their data is underpowered for small groups such as recent graduates. The two results are compatible.

options.html: The payroll finding proves the economy-wide result is mistaken
options.text: The payroll finding proves the economy-wide result is mistaken
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. The payroll study itself reports no evidence of economy-wide displacement. An effect limited to one small group may not show in economy-wide totals.

options.html: Both results show that AI has caused widespread job losses so far
options.text: Both results show that AI has caused widespread job losses so far
options.feedbackHtml: Sorry, that's incorrect. Neither shows that. One finds no significant effect, and the other finds a descriptive gap in one group, which may not show in economy-wide totals.

title: Jobs, tasks, and productivity
